source.title: CDR: Customizable Density Ratios of Strong-over-weak LLMs for Preference Annotation
source.authors: Guangxuan Xu; Kai Xu; Shivchander Sudalairaj; Hao Wang; Akash Srivastava

page_placements.theme: Weak AI feedback (preference labels, density-ratio rewards, corrections, judge or peer-prediction rewards) for alignment training of a stronger policy

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some table content is flattened, so ambiguous values are not assigned to specific rows.
record.tranche_reason: The study builds Dr.SoW, a preference-annotation method based on strong/weak model density ratios, and reports how that method performs. It does not test fine-tuning a strong student directly on labels from a weak supervisor or measure PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports reward-benchmark results and downstream preference-tuning results for its own density-ratio annotation method. These do not measure the weak-to-strong student-versus-supervisor effect or PGR, so none of the claim versions is tested. Results from other studies cited in the paper are not included.
record.test_reason: The study builds a preference reward from the log-density ratio of a better-aligned over a less-aligned LLM (Dr.SoW). It reports RewardBench accuracy and downstream SimPO results for that reward. It never trains a strong student on a weaker supervisor's labels to compare the two, and reports no PGR or strong ceiling. The 'strong-over-weak' pairing is a different construct from weak-to-strong generalization. Its 'Weak-to-strong generalization' related-work paragraph discusses contrastive decoding and ExPO, and the original (arXiv:2312.09390) is not in its references. So it neither tests nor uses the claim; it only discusses the area (T6, not T4).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that density ratios from pairs with a larger alignment gap give better preference rewards (their 'Strong-over-Weak hypothesis'). Domain-specific instructions and routing improve reward quality further without training. Dr.SoW-annotated data lifts Llama-3-8B-Instruct to results competitive with SoTA reward classifiers and near GPT-4 level on ArenaHard.
record.recipe_differences: The study scores responses using a strong/weak model log-density ratio, optionally conditioned on domain instructions, then uses the resulting preferences for SimPO. It does not directly train a strong student on labels emitted by a weak supervisor or calculate PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Reward quality varies with the alignment gap and choice of denominator model; prompt instructions and domain routing also change reward results. The paper reports that an overly long safety prompt can reduce performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 221 Llama-8B and Mistral-7B pairs, density-ratio reward accuracy on RewardBench rises with the ArenaHard gap between numerator and denominator. It is near 50% at zero gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A log-density-ratio reward is more accurate when the numerator model is much better aligned than the denominator model.

fits_no_version.finding: Llama-3-8B-Instruct SimPO-tuned on density-ratio-annotated data improves over the starting model. LC AlpacaEval goes 22.9 to 39.9/40.7 and ArenaHard 22.3 to 34.6/37.4. The SFT-vs-Base pair gives little gain (23.3/23.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference data annotated by a strong-over-weak density ratio improves a policy, and only when the pair's alignment gap is large.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain-customized density ratio scores 82.6 on RewardBench with a router and 84.9 with oracle routing, versus 77.2 without instructions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-conditioning the density ratio with domain instructions and ICL examples improves reward accuracy.

record.problems: The paper does not measure PGR, compare the fine-tuned student directly against the weak supervisor, or report a strong-model ceiling for that comparison. The principal reward-quality finding is described as a correlation, with no uncertainty estimates stated. Some table values are flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Other Table 1 reward-benchmark values and Table 2 training results were not separately extracted because they are comparisons of the paper's annotation pipeline and the flattened table does not reliably assign all values to conditions and metrics.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from uses_without_test/T4 to discusses/T6. The paper does not rely on the weak-to-strong finding as a tool, and it does not cite the original. The shared 'strong/weak' wording is coincidental; the construct here is a reward built from two models' likelihood ratio. All rows correctly link to no version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a strong student trained on a weaker model's labels beats that supervisor, and PGR.
Whether training changes raise PGR over naive weak-label fine-tuning.
PGR variation by supervisor/student size, task, or representation. The paper instead studies alignment gap versus density-ratio reward quality.
The stated weak-to-strong failure modes and their effects on PGR.
Theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.

relation.reason: Its related-work discussion covers contrasting strong and weak models, but its experiments do not test any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates density-ratio preference annotation and downstream SimPO performance. It neither tests nor relies on the catalog's weak-supervisor-to-strong-student effect.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is Dr. SoW, arXiv v3 dated 31 January 2025; its title differs from the pack. These downstream method results provide neither PGR nor a comparison against a weak supervisor; the statement's 23.3/23.5 values describe vanilla SFT-over-Base.
